title: Chapter 148 – The Gardener's Hundredth Year
html:
[Lin Garden – Lin Wenyuan]

On the morning of his hundredth birthday Lin Wenyuan wakes up warm, which is the first sign that something is wrong.

His hands have been cold for sixteen years. It is not the cold of winter. It is a deep, patient, mineral chill that lives in the bones of the fingers, and it has never left him since the night in the Orchard when he broke through to the middle Foundation and the heat went out of him like air from a bellows. He has worn mittens in summer. He has slept with hot stones in his bed. He has learned to hold his tea in the crook of his elbow, so that his wife does not see how it trembles.

This morning, in the thin light of dawn, he lies on his back under the quilt and flexes his fingers, and they are warm.

He lies there for a long time without moving. He is afraid to move. Beside him, in the narrow bed that they have shared for seventy-six years, Qinghe sleeps with her mouth a little open and one hand curled under her cheek, looking about thirty-five. He listens to her breathe. He lifts his right hand and holds it in front of his face, and the light from the shutter makes a bright blur of the fingers, and he thinks, quite clearly: Oh. So that's what it feels like.

Then he sneezes, and everything is ordinary again.

* * *

The birthday is not a large affair, because he has forbidden it.

He has been forbidding it for a month. He says that a man of a hundred has no business being fussed over. He says that the cost of the cake could feed a family of ten for a week. He says a number of other things, in his most dignified voice, and then he comes into the long hall at noon in his good blue gown and finds two hundred and forty Lins waiting, with a cake the size of a cart wheel, and sits down very quietly in the chair they have put at the head of the table and does not say a word.

"Speech," says Qinghe.

"I have nothing to say."

"You have always something to say. You say it at supper every night for an hour."

"That is complaining. This is a speech." He looks around the table, at the faces of his grandchildren and their children and their children's children, the great tribe of them, all with the same stubborn straight eyebrows, most of whom he could not name, and his throat does something unexpected. "I was born in a village called Green Pine Hill, the son of a man who grew apples and lost his orchard. I had nothing. I had a cart and a wife and a baby. I thought, if I can keep these three alive until spring..." He stops. His voice has gone strange. "I have kept a great many people alive until spring. I find I am not sorry."

There is a silence. Then Lin Kuang, nine months old and seated on his mother's knee, bangs a spoon on the table and says "Ba!" with tremendous firmness, and the entire hall dissolves.

The cake is excellent. He has three pieces. He has noticed that Qinghe has given him a very small look every time he reaches for the knife, and he ignores it every time, with the good conscience of a man who has been hungry before.

Afterward, in the corridor, Jian catches his arm.

"Father."

"Little stone."

"Your hands."

"Ah." Wenyuan holds them up, turning them over. "Warm. I was going to tell you. They have been warm since this morning. I thought it might be the cake."

Jian looks at the hands. He looks at them for an unnecessarily long time. His white hair is tied back and the lines in his face are deep as plow furrows, but when he lifts his head the old stricken look has crossed it, and Wenyuan, who has seen that look before, in a burning orchard, over a woman's body, puts his hand firmly on his son's shoulder.

"It is not a disaster."

"It is a sign."

"Of what?"

"That it is time." Jian's voice is low. "A hundred is the number. The Foundation Middle gives a body a hundred years. Anyone who goes past it without a step..." He cannot finish.

"I know," says Wenyuan gently. "I have known for some time. I did not want to spoil the cake."

* * *

The Head sends for him that evening.

It is a small private summons, delivered by a pupil of the Law benches with a bow and a basket of persimmons. Wenyuan climbs the ridge in the dusk, on his apple-wood staff, with Pebble riding on his shoulder, and the old stone creature is quiet for most of the way, which is how he knows that Pebble knows.

Yan Rongzhi is waiting in the Founders' Chamber.

It is a round high room at the top of the ridge-house, with a floor of black jade and a dome of pale gray stone, and in the center of it stands a single slab, long and low, polished by seventy years of a sleeper's weight. The Head sits beside it in his wooden chair. There is a lamp on the floor and a cup of tea on his knee, and when Wenyuan comes in, he rises, slowly, with a hand on the chair, and bows.

"Elder Lin."

"Master Yan." Wenyuan bows in return, with some difficulty. "You didn't have to get up."

"I did." The black eyes are warm. "I have not met a man of a hundred before. I find I am nervous."

"I find it less exciting than they say."

Yan Rongzhi laughs, softly. It is a pleasant, rusty sound. He lowers himself back into the chair and gestures, and Wenyuan takes the stool opposite, and for a little while they sit in the lamp-light, two old men with teacups, and do not talk of anything important.

Then the Head sets down his cup.

"I have something for you."

"I thought you might."

"I have been awake eleven years. I have spent them being useful, and also, I confess, being a nuisance." The thin face crinkles. "But all this time I have kept a secret. I have not told your son. I did not wish to put it in his hands, because he is the sort of man who would try to give it to everyone."

He opens his left fist.

In the palm lies a small round thing, no larger than a pea. It is pale, translucent, faintly milky, like a pearl, and as Wenyuan looks at it he realizes that it is faintly moving. There is a slow shifting light inside it, like a very small dream.

"When I lay down on that slab," says the Head, "I did a thing the old Keepers never did. I did not simply sleep. I held on. For seventy years I kept something of myself, a small clear place, a kind of breath, behind the sleep. I did not know why. I thought it a conceit." He turns the pearl in his fingers. "It turns out that if one holds a breath long enough, with the gold of the Fire burning on one side and the dark of the Gate pressing on the other, it condenses. This is seventy years of an honest man's waking sleep. It has no name. It might feed a Core. It might heal a wound that is a century old."

"Master Yan—"

"It would carry you from the Middle to the Late stage of the Foundation. Perhaps further. It would give you thirty years. Perhaps fifty." He closes his hand. "Do you want it?"

"No," says Wenyuan.

The Head blinks.

"I mean to say, thank you. I am honored. But I think you should keep it for someone who is needed." He spreads his cold-no-longer hands on his knees. "I am a hundred. I have lived four times as long as any Lin before me. My son has given up a Seed's worth of years to keep me. I do not think I can take any more."

"Elder—"

"I am not being modest. I am being practical." He smiles. "What would a man do with fifty years? I would grow apples. I would tell the same stories. I would sit at the head of the table at supper and grumble. It would be a pleasant life, and it would take food from some child's mouth."

"I see." The Head studies him for a long moment. "May I tell you why I do not accept that?"

"Please."

"Because I know what the gift costs." Yan Rongzhi's voice is very gentle. "I know exactly what it costs. I carried it. It is the only part of me that I made on purpose." He lifts the pearl, and the light inside it shivers. "When I give it away, I give away the last of what has kept me awake. I do not think I shall wake up again. I think, in truth, I shall go to sleep, quite easily, and not be afraid."

Wenyuan goes very still.

"You would die."

"I would finish." The Head smiles. "I am a hundred and seventy-three years old, Elder. I have lived in a great many centuries. I was a boy with a sword. I was Head of this Sect for sixty-three years. I slept seventy and woke to see my oldest friend's great-great-grandchildren growing apples on my mountain." His eyes are bright. "I would very much like to be of use to a man I like. I find that wish is a great deal stronger than the wish to keep going. It is, I think, what I have been waiting for."

* * *

He does not decide on the mountain.

He walks home in the dark, with Pebble humming quietly on his shoulder, and when he reaches the long low house he finds Qinghe sitting up in the kitchen with a lamp and a pot of tea. She does not say anything. She pours him a cup. He sits across the table, and she looks at his hands, and her sharp small eyes soften.

"They're warm," she says.

"I told you."

"You did not tell me. I felt it. In the night." She reaches across and takes them both. Hers are small and strong and rough. "How long have you had?"

"A month, perhaps. Maybe two."

"And you did not say."

"I did not want to spoil the cake."

She laughs. It is a short sharp sound, half a sob. Then she turns his hands over and presses her thumbs into the palms, hard, as she has done every morning of their marriage when his fingers were stiff, and he feels the warmth of them go through his whole arm.

"Wenyuan."

"Yes?"

"I have been married to you seventy-six years."

"It has been a pleasure."

"It has been trying." She doesn't look up. "You are the most stubborn, long-winded, impractical man I ever met. I have wanted to hit you with a ladle on at least four thousand occasions. I want you to take the Head's pearl."

"Qinghe—"

"No. Listen." She raises her eyes. They are fierce and wet. "He is offering. He wishes to. If you say no, you take that from him. It is not yours to take. You tell me that you are being practical. You are being a coward." Her voice breaks. "You have spent a hundred years giving everything you had to whoever walked in the door. This is the first time anyone has offered you something back. Be gracious. Say yes."

He stares at her.

"I do not know how," he admits.

"I'll teach you." She smiles through the tears. "It's very simple. You open your mouth, and you say thank you, and you do not argue."

* * *

They hold the ceremony on the night of the winter solstice, in the Founders' Chamber, with only five in attendance.

The Head lies on the slab. He has asked for it. He lies on his back in his green robe, with his hands crossed on his chest and his white hair spread on the black jade, and he looks, Wenyuan thinks, absurdly young. There is a lamp at his head and a lamp at his feet. Qinghe sits at one side, on a stool, with her hand resting on the old man's wrist. Jian stands at the other, in his brown cloak, silent and sorrowful, with the Seed's gold shining faintly in his eyes. Pebble is on the floor. Head Han, who has come to witness, stands by the door with the jade seal in her hand and an expression of grave stillness.

Wenyuan kneels beside the slab.

"It is not complicated," says the Head. "I shall put it into your hand. You will swallow it. It will go to the same place the Fire went, in my chest, and it will settle there, and your breath will take it. I would advise against moving."

"Master Yan." Wenyuan's voice shakes. "I do not know what to say."

"Say what Qinghe told you."

"Thank you."

"That's it." The thin face creases with pleasure. "That's the whole of it. You see? You are better at it than you think."

He opens his left hand. The pearl lies in it, pale and moving, no bigger than a pea. It is lighter than anything Wenyuan has ever held. He takes it between finger and thumb. It is warm, like a living thing, and as he lifts it toward his mouth he hears, quite clearly, a faint whisper, as of a very old man talking in his sleep.

Tend the tree.

He swallows.

* * *

It is not a flood or a fire or a fall.

It is a waking. He feels it begin at the center of him, a small warm place under his breastbone, where the cold had been. It spreads, slowly, like ink in water. It runs along his arms and legs. It finds the old broken places, the cracked ribs from his twenties, the bad knee, the scar across his back where the roof beam fell, and it eases them, one by one, as a mother eases a child's cramped hand. His breath deepens. His heart, which has been beating for a hundred years with a slight stumble, steadies.

And the world goes wide.

He is standing in an orchard. It is not his own. The trees are enormous and very old, with trunks as thick as houses, and the grass beneath them is silver in the moonlight. Beyond the trees there is a hill. On the hill there is a small stone house, and at the door of the house a tall man in a blue smock is kneeling on one knee, with a seedling in a clay pot.

He is tall and stooped, with spectacles pushed up on his forehead and a short untidy beard. His hands are long. There is a scar across the left palm, white and old. A child stands in front of him, a girl of perhaps seven, in a ragged tunic, with enormous dark eyes. She is holding out both hands.

You will not see the end of it, says the man, in a voice that is tired and kind and a little frightened. I am sorry. It is a long way. But it is a good tree. It will bear fruit for a very long time.

What is it for? says the girl.

It's for someone. He smiles. Someone who is not here yet. Someone who is, I think, going to be very lonely. He puts the pot in her hands. When he comes, tell him he was wanted. Tell him that even though I did not know his name. Will you do that?

Yes, says the girl.

Good girl. He rises, with a groan. Tend the tree.

The vision fades. The orchard is gone. Wenyuan is kneeling on the black jade floor, with his hands on his thighs and the tears running down his face, and the lamp is guttering, and the Head's hand is cold in his.

* * *

"Master Yan?"

The old man's eyes are open. He is looking at the dome of the chamber, at the pale gray stone, at the single slanting beam of starlight falling through the oculus. He looks calm. He looks, in fact, entirely happy.

"Did it work?" he says.

"I think so."

"Good." A breath. "Did you see?"

"I saw." Wenyuan swallows. "A man in a blue smock. A little girl."

"Ah." The Head's face softens. "Yes. I thought you might. It's the pearl. It carries what it's been near." His fingers tighten, weakly, on Wenyuan's. "I have been dreaming him for seventy years. I never knew his name. I only knew that he was sorry."

"He was."

"He built a trap and he was sorry." The black eyes drift toward Jian, standing on the far side of the slab, white-haired, with his hands at his sides. "Keeper."

"Master."

"Come here." Jian kneels. The Head looks at him for a long time, with the fond sharp attention of a teacher regarding a pupil he has outlasted. "I told you the Gate was a door that was never finished. I was wrong. I have had a long time to think about it." He coughs. "It is not a door. It is a mouth. It has been trying to say something for six hundred years. It could not find anyone who would listen."

"What does it say?"

"I do not know." The thin lips curve. "But you have a sister who hears. And a father who dreams. And a mother who cooks in the dark. You have, I think, the best chance anyone has ever had." His hand closes on Jian's wrist. "Do not open it for him. The one you are afraid of. Do not open it for the man in the blue smock."

"Master—"

"Open it for the child." His eyes flutter. "The one who is, I think, still waiting."

Jian's face changes. Wenyuan sees it, from where he kneels: a quick terrible stillness, like a man hearing his name called in an empty house.

"Which child?" Jian whispers.

But Yan Rongzhi has closed his eyes. He is smiling, a little. His chest rises, once, and falls, and does not rise again. The lamp at his head goes out.

Outside, on the ridge, a bell begins to ring.

* * *

They bury him in the apple orchard, beside Kuang, in the hard cold dawn.

It is a large funeral. Half the Sect comes, and all the Lins, and Pei An and Pei Wanli, and old Gu Mingzhe in his butter-colored robe, who weeps openly into a silk handkerchief. Head Han speaks, in her cold dry voice, and says only that Yan Rongzhi was the last Head to sleep, and the first to wake, and that the Sect owes him a debt which it does not have the coin to pay. Wuping stands at the back with a stick and a cough, and holds the hand of a child.

Before the first earth falls, a tall scarred man in a stained smock comes shyly through the crowd with a roll of paper under his arm. It is Ning Ruiyan. He has walked down from the observatory in the dark. He bows to Qinghe, then to Jian, and says in a low rough voice that he would not intrude, but he thought the Keeper would wish to know.

"The ring," he says. "The eleven stars. They went dark last night. Not at the third watch, as they do. At the first. And they stayed dark until dawn."

Jian does not move. "How long?"

"Five hours. Last year it was two." Ning unrolls the paper, and shows a column of tiny figures, the nights and hours of nine years, each one a little longer than the last. "It is getting wider. Whatever stands in front of the gap. It is coming closer."

Qinghe takes Jian's arm. Nobody says anything. At the grave's edge, the first flakes of snow come drifting down onto the new black earth.

Wenyuan stands at the front, at the lip of the grave.

His hands are warm. He holds them out in front of him, in the thin morning light, and looks at them: spotted, knotted, a hundred years old and no longer cold. Beside him Qinghe stands very straight in her blue smock, and does not weep, and does not let go of his arm.

He feels the new strength in his chest, the quiet breath of the Late stage. It is a good strength. It will give him thirty years. He does not feel it as he expected to. He feels, instead, a deep and curious sleepiness, a heaviness behind the eyes, as though the pearl had left a little of its seventy years behind in him, and some part of him is already beginning to dream.

Tend the tree, he thinks. Yes. All right.

He takes a handful of earth, and lets it fall.

* * *

He is asleep before supper.

It happens at the table, in the long hall, in the middle of a sentence. He is telling Lin Kuang's father a story about a cow, and his eyes close, and his head sinks gently onto his chest. Nobody panics. Qinghe, who has been waiting for it all day, lays down her spoon, fetches a quilt, and tucks it around his shoulders with a sharp brisk tenderness. "There," she says. "Let him."

"How long?" says Zhao, in a whisper.

"Until the thaw."

Jian has come in from the Dock. He stands at the foot of the table in his brown cloak, looking at his father's sleeping face. The long jaw has gone slack. The mouth is a little open. In the lamp-light he looks as he looked in the oldest picture Jian can remember, a thin quiet man on a cart, asleep with his hat over his eyes.

"It is the cost," says Jian.

"Yes."

"The Head said the pearl would leave something. I did not think it would be this."

"It is not so bad." Qinghe smooths the quilt. "He will wake in spring. He will be warm, and well, and very hungry. And every winter after, he will sleep. That is all." Her mouth trembles, once. "He has been awake for a hundred years. I think he is owed a rest."

Jian crouches beside the chair. He takes his father's hand, and it is warm in his, large and spotted and calloused, and it closes, in sleep, around his fingers.

"Father," he says, very quietly. "I have to tell you something. I do not think you can hear."

Wenyuan's lips move. It might be a word. It might be nothing.

"There is someone else in me," says Jian. "I do not know who. The interface says there are two. I think... I think it is a child. I think he has been there all along, and that I have been walking about in his life, and that I never once thought to ask his name." His voice cracks. "I am afraid I stole it. I am afraid there was a boy, and that I took his place, and that he has been waiting at the end of a corridor for fifty years."

Silence. The fire pops. Then, from the depth of the quilt, in a slow thick sleeping murmur, comes a sentence so clear that Qinghe's head snaps round.

"Well, little stone," says Wenyuan. "Then I have two."

He does not wake. He sighs, and settles, and the hand in Jian's tightens once.

Jian puts his forehead against it. He stays there, kneeling on the boards, white head bent, for a long, long time. Qinghe stands over him with her hand on his hair, and the lamp burns down, and outside the first snow begins to fall.
